nameStory: The variegated fritillary gets its name from the beautiful, varied patchwork of colors decorating its wings - orange, brown, and black in an intricate checkerboard pattern. 'Variegated' means having different colors arranged in patches or spots, which perfectly describes this butterfly's distinctive wing design. The word 'fritillary' comes from the Latin word for a dice box, referring to the checkered pattern that all fritillaries share.
description: The variegated fritillary is a medium-sized butterfly with striking orange wings decorated with black spots and lines in a checkerboard pattern. Unlike many butterflies, it lacks the silvery spots on the underwings that other fritillaries typically have. These butterflies are known for their restless, nomadic nature - they rarely stay in one place for long and are constantly on the move. They're swift, low-flying butterflies that can be quite challenging to approach or photograph.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Orange wings with distinct black checkered markings and spots, but notably lacking the silvery spots on the underwing that most other fritillaries have

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: Fast, low, and erratic flight pattern that stays close to the ground, darting quickly from flower to flower

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely skittish and difficult to approach - they'll fly away at the slightest movement or shadow, living up to their scientific name meaning 'easily scared'

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Forewings are more pointed and angular compared to the rounded wings of other fritillaries, giving them a slightly different silhouette in flight

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized butterfly with wings spanning about 2-3 inches, smaller than great spangled fritillaries but larger than pearl crescents

habitat: Variegated fritillaries prefer open, sunny areas like fields, meadows, prairies, and roadsides where wildflowers are abundant. They're particularly drawn to areas with passionflowers, violets, and other low-growing plants that serve as host plants for their caterpillars. You'll often find them in disturbed habitats like old fields, gardens, and along sunny woodland edges where flowers are plentiful.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring as temperatures warm, with the first generation emerging from overwintering pupae to seek out early wildflowers for nectar.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in summer when you'll see multiple generations flying simultaneously, with adults constantly searching for mates and egg-laying sites on host plants.
seasonality.fall: Late summer and early fall bring the final generation of the year, with these individuals often the most numerous as they prepare for winter by either migrating south or entering dormancy.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity in New England winters - they survive as pupae in protected locations or may migrate southward to warmer regions.

funFact: The variegated fritillary is such a nervous butterfly that its scientific genus name 'Euptoieta' literally means 'easily scared' in Greek - and it lives up to this reputation by being one of the most difficult butterflies to photograph or observe closely in the wild!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with great spangled fritillaries, but variegated fritillaries lack the distinctive silvery spots on the underwings that great spangled fritillaries have. Memory trick: 'Variegated' means varied colors but NO silver - if you see silver spots underneath, it's not a variegated fritillary.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a fritillary, the variegated fritillary is quite different from other New England fritillaries in behavior and ecology - it's nomadic rather than staying in one area, has multiple broods per year instead of just one, and uses a much wider variety of host plants including passionflowers, which links it more closely to tropical butterflies.
compareHints: Since it's the only member of its genus in New England, compare it to other fritillaries in the brush-footed butterfly family. Unlike great spangled and other Speyeria fritillaries, variegated fritillaries are much more restless and mobile, have multiple generations per year instead of just one, and completely lack the silver spots on their underwings. They're also generally smaller and have more pointed forewings than their Speyeria cousins.
